traveler: Aaron the Levite, son of Amram, first high priest of Israel
title: The Mouth of Moses and the Rod That Blossomed: Goshen to Mount Hor
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The House of Amram in Goshen

stops.name: Goshen, the elder brother born
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Exodus 7:7 fixes the three-year gap with Moses, and this file follows the rabbinic chronology used elsewhere in the corpus (Exodus c. 1313 BC). The 1 Kings 6:1 reckoning would place the birth c. 1529 BC instead. Scripture gives no calendar year and does not name Goshen as the birthplace; the setting is inferred from Genesis 47:27.
stops.campa: In the land of Goshen, where the sons of Israel keep their flocks under an Egypt that has forgotten Joseph, Jochebed bears a son to Amram of the tribe of Levi and they call him Aaron. The house counts its descent through Kohath and Levi and Jacob back to Abraham, and it has been four generations in Egypt. He is the second child; Miriam is older. Three years later a third will be born and hidden in the reeds, and the whole weight of the story will fall on that one. For those three years he is the only son in the house of Amram.
suggested_refs: The eastern Nile Delta settlement of Goshen, Genesis 47:27, land of the Israelite sojourn

stops.name: Goshen, the decree that comes three years too late
stops.date_confidence: rabbinic tradition, not scripture. The decree is dated to the year of Moses's birth by b. Sotah 12a and Exodus Rabbah 1:13, with Seder Olam Rabbah supplying the three-year interval; Exodus 1:22 gives no date at all.
stops.campa: Pharaoh gives the order that every son born to the Hebrews is to be cast into the river. The rabbis reckon the decree falls in the year of Moses's birth, three years after Aaron's, and so it passes over the elder brother entirely: he is already walking, already too old to be counted a newborn. He grows up in the open while his brother grows up first in a basket and then in a palace. Nothing in the text says what he made of that. The Torah gives Aaron no childhood, and picks him up again at eighty-three.
suggested_refs: b. Sotah 12a and Exodus Rabbah 1:13 on the timing of Pharaoh's decree

stops.name: Goshen, Elisheba daughter of Amminadab
stops.date_confidence: undated in the sources; the marriage is recorded in a genealogy with no chronology attached, and the position here is narrative order only.
stops.campa: Aaron takes to wife Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon, who will carry the standard of Judah out of Egypt. The priestly house and the royal tribe are joined in one household before either exists. She bears him four sons: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, Ithamar, named in that order in every list, and the order will matter. Two of them will be ash on the day the sanctuary opens; the other two carry the line. Of Elisheba scripture records nothing else, not her death, not one word she speaks.
suggested_refs: The genealogy of Levi in Exodus 6:14-27, the only family record given for Aaron

stops.name: Horeb, the brother sent into the wilderness
stops.date_confidence: traditional; placed between the burning bush and the return to Egypt in the corpus chronology of Moses. The text supplies sequence, not dates.
stops.campa: At the far mountain his brother stands before a bush that burns and is not consumed, arguing that he is slow of speech and slow of tongue. The answer comes back as a fact already in motion: Aaron is on the road. He walks out of Egypt into the wilderness without being told why, meets Moses at the mountain of God, and kisses him. The elder brother is eighty-three. Moses tells him all the words of the Lord that had sent him, and all the signs he had been commanded.
stops.quote: Is not Aaron the Levite thy brother? I know that he can speak well.
suggested_refs: The traditional Horeb of Jebel Musa in south Sinai, meeting place of the brothers

stops.name: Goshen, the elders of Israel gathered
stops.date_confidence: traditional; sequence from Exodus 4:29-31, no date in the text.
stops.campa: The brothers come back into Egypt and gather all the elders of the children of Israel. Moses has the words; Aaron speaks them, and does the signs in the sight of the people. The rod, the hand made leprous and healed, water taken from the river. The people believe, and when they hear that the Lord has looked upon their affliction they bow their heads and worship. Within the week Pharaoh has doubled the burden on them, and the same men meet the brothers coming out from the king and say, the Lord look upon you, and judge.
suggested_refs: The assembly of the elders of Israel, Exodus 4:29-31

stops.name: Pi-Ramesses, eighty-three years old before Pharaoh
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the ages in Exodus 7:7 are attested, the calendar date is not. The court's location is a scholarly identification with Pi-Ramesses at Qantir, not a scriptural one.
stops.campa: Aaron is eighty-three and Moses eighty when they come in to Pharaoh. Aaron is the voice: thus saith the Lord God of Israel, let my people go. The king of Egypt has never heard of this god and says so, and orders that the straw be withheld while the tale of bricks stands, and the officers of the children of Israel are beaten for the shortfall. Afterward the Lord tells Moses, see, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet. The title given to him is prophet.
suggested_refs: Qantir, the Ramesside royal residence, leading candidate for the Exodus-era court

stops.name: Pi-Ramesses, the rod that swallows rods
stops.date_confidence: traditional; sequence only.
stops.campa: Pharaoh asks for a wonder. Aaron casts down his rod before the throne and it becomes a serpent, and the wise men and the sorcerers of Egypt cast down theirs and theirs become serpents too. The court has seen this trick before. Then Aaron's rod swallows their rods, and the magicians have nothing further to say. The heart of Pharaoh hardens anyway, exactly as it was foretold that it would. The rod goes back into Aaron's hand. He will use it again on the river and on the dust of the ground.
stops.quote: For they cast down every man his rod, and they became serpents: but Aaron's rod swallowed up their rods.
suggested_refs: The contest of the rods before Pharaoh, Exodus 7:8-13

segments.name: The Plagues and the Going Out

stops.name: The Nile, the water turned
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the corpus chronology of the plagues, which the text does not date.
stops.campa: By the water's edge in the morning, in the sight of Pharaoh and of his servants, Moses gives the word and Aaron lifts the rod and smites the river. The Nile turns to blood, and the streams and the ponds and all the pools of standing water with it; the fish die, the river stinks, and Egypt digs round about the river for water to drink. The god of the country is the river. Aaron's hand does the striking; the words that call the plague down are not his. Seven days the water stays foul.
suggested_refs: The first plague, Exodus 7:19-25

stops.name: Egypt, frogs and the dust made lice
stops.date_confidence: traditional; sequence only.
stops.campa: He stretches the rod over the streams and the frogs come up and cover the land, into the ovens and the kneading troughs and the bedchambers of the king. He smites the dust of the earth and the dust becomes lice throughout all the borders of Egypt, upon man and upon beast. Here the magicians break: they try with their enchantments and cannot, and they say to Pharaoh, this is the finger of God. Pharaoh's heart is hardened notwithstanding, and he hearkens not unto them, as the Lord had said.
suggested_refs: The second and third plagues, Exodus 8:1-19

stops.name: Egypt, ashes of the furnace thrown toward heaven
stops.date_confidence: traditional; sequence only.
stops.campa: For the sixth plague the two brothers stand together at a furnace and take handfuls of its ashes, and Moses throws them toward heaven in the sight of Pharaoh. The dust goes out over all the land as a boil breaking forth with blains upon man and upon beast, and the magicians cannot stand before Moses, because the boil is upon them as well. Aaron carries the ash and does not throw it. It is the last of the ten plagues in which he does anything at all.
suggested_refs: The sixth plague, Exodus 9:8-12, the only later plague in which Aaron acts

stops.name: Rameses, the going out
stops.date_confidence: attested as an internal biblical date (fifteenth day of the first month, Numbers 33:3); the absolute year is traditional.
stops.campa: On the fifteenth day of the first month, the morning after the blood on the doorposts and the cry that goes up in every Egyptian house, they journey from Rameses toward Succoth: six hundred thousand on foot beside children, a mixed multitude with them, flocks and herds, and dough unleavened on their shoulders because they were thrust out and could not tarry. The ordinance of the Passover was spoken to Moses and to Aaron together, the two of them addressed as one. Aaron is eighty-three years old on the road.
suggested_refs: Numbers 33:3, the itinerary's own dating of the departure from Rameses

stops.name: Succoth, the first camp outside Egypt
stops.date_confidence: internal biblical sequence; the identification of Succoth with Tell el-Maskhuta in the Wadi Tumilat is a leading archaeological guess, not certain.
stops.campa: The first camp out of Egypt is at Succoth on the edge of the cultivated land, booths thrown up for a night, a whole nation sleeping outside a border for the first time in four hundred years. From here the Lord goes before them in a pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night, and they turn south rather than take the short road along the sea. Aaron travels in the body of the people, not at the head of it. He is not named again until the second month.
suggested_refs: Tell el-Maskhuta in the Wadi Tumilat, candidate site for Succoth

stops.name: Pi-hahiroth, the sea before them and the chariots behind
stops.date_confidence: internal biblical sequence. The crossing point is among the most disputed sites in biblical geography; these coordinates follow the traditional identification with Ayun Musa used across the corpus.
stops.campa: They encamp before Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, and the chariots of Egypt come up behind them at evening. The people cry out against Moses: were there no graves in Egypt. The sea divides at his hand, not Aaron's, and the host goes over on dry ground between two walls of water while the pillar of fire stands behind them through the night. Aaron crosses in the crowd with his wife and his four sons, none of them named in the account, one man among six hundred thousand walking on the floor of a sea.
suggested_refs: Ayun Musa, the Wells of Moses, traditional site of the crossing

stops.name: Marah, the bitter water
stops.date_confidence: internal biblical sequence; the identification with Ain Hawarah is traditional and the published coordinates for it vary by some twenty-five kilometres.
stops.campa: Three days into the wilderness of Shur they find no water, and the water they do find at Marah is bitter and cannot be drunk. The people murmur against Moses, and this is the first of the murmurings; there will be one at nearly every camp between here and the fortieth year. The Lord shows Moses a tree; he casts it into the water and the water is made sweet. Aaron is not named in the account at all. There the Lord makes a statute and an ordinance for them, and proves them, saying, I am the Lord that healeth thee.
suggested_refs: Ain Hawarah, the traditional Marah, a brackish spring southeast of Suez

stops.name: Elim, twelve wells and threescore and ten palm trees
stops.date_confidence: internal biblical sequence; Wadi Gharandel is the traditional identification, unverified.
stops.campa: At Elim there are twelve wells of water and threescore and ten palm trees, and the whole company camps there by the water. The number of the wells is the number of the tribes, and the number of the palms is the number of the elders who will one day eat and drink before God on the mountain; nobody in the camp remarks on it. It is simply a good place, with shade and enough to drink for the people and for the herds. They stay by the wells, and then move on into the wilderness of Sin.
suggested_refs: Wadi Gharandel, oasis identified by tradition with Elim

stops.name: The wilderness of Sin, the murmuring against Moses and Aaron
stops.date_confidence: attested as an internal biblical date (fifteenth day of the second month, Exodus 16:1); the plain of Debbet er-Ramleh is the common but unproven candidate.
stops.campa: On the fifteenth day of the second month the whole congregation murmurs against Moses and against Aaron: would to God we had died by the flesh pots of Egypt, where we did eat bread to the full. The two answer together, your murmurings are not against us but against the Lord, and while Aaron speaks to the congregation the glory of the Lord appears in the cloud. That evening the quails come up and cover the camp. In the morning a small round thing lies upon the face of the wilderness, like hoar frost on the ground.
suggested_refs: The Debbet er-Ramleh plain, candidate for the wilderness of Sin

stops.name: Rephidim, the hands held up until the going down of the sun
stops.date_confidence: internal biblical sequence; the Feiran oasis is a strong traditional candidate for Rephidim, not a fixed one.
stops.campa: Amalek comes against Israel at Rephidim, and Moses goes up the hill with the rod of God in his hand while Joshua fights in the valley. When Moses holds up his hand Israel prevails; when he lets it down Amalek prevails, and his hands grow heavy. Aaron and Hur put a stone under him and set him on it, and hold up his hands, the one on the one side and the other on the other side, and his hands are steady until the going down of the sun. What the two of them said to each other on that hilltop is not recorded.
suggested_refs: Wadi Feiran and its oasis, traditional Rephidim

stops.name: Sinai, the elders eat and drink before God
stops.date_confidence: traditional; third month after the Exodus per Exodus 19:1, the day itself unfixed.
stops.campa: Aaron goes up the mountain with Nadab and Abihu and seventy of the elders of Israel, so far and no further, while Moses alone goes on into the cloud. They see the God of Israel, and under his feet as it were a paved work of a sapphire stone, and as it were the body of heaven in its clearness. Upon the nobles of Israel he lays not his hand: they see God, and eat and drink. Two of the men at that meal will be dead within the year, killed by fire from the same presence they are eating in front of.
suggested_refs: The plain of er-Raha below Jebel Musa, traditional camp of Israel at Sinai

stops.name: Sinai, garments for glory and for beauty
stops.date_confidence: traditional; placed within the forty days of Exodus 24:18, which the text does not subdivide.
stops.campa: On the mountain the Lord dictates the clothing of a man who does not yet know he is to be clothed: the ephod of gold and blue and purple and scarlet, the breastplate of judgment with twelve stones cut like a signet, each graven with the name of a tribe, the Urim and the Thummim set inside it, the robe with bells and pomegranates along its hem so that his sound is heard when he goes into the holy place, the mitre with a plate of pure gold. All of it is measured to Aaron, down to the linen breeches.
stops.quote: And thou shalt make holy garments for Aaron thy brother for glory and for beauty.
suggested_refs: The specification of the priestly vestments, Exodus 28 and Exodus 39

stops.name: Er-Raha below Sinai, the golden calf
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the seventeenth of Tammuz is the rabbinic dating of the broken tables, not a date given in Exodus.
stops.campa: Moses has been forty days on the mountain and the people gather themselves against Aaron: make us gods which shall go before us, for as for this Moses, we know not what is become of him. He asks them for the golden earrings in the ears of their wives and their sons and their daughters. He takes what they bring, fashions it with a graving tool, and makes a molten calf, and they say, these be thy gods, O Israel. Then Aaron builds an altar before it and makes a proclamation, and the proclamation is not to the calf.
stops.quote: To morrow is a feast to the Lord.
suggested_refs: Nicolas Poussin, The Adoration of the Golden Calf, National Gallery, London

stops.name: Sinai, there came out this calf
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the day after the calf in narrative sequence.
stops.campa: Moses comes down, breaks the tables at the foot of the mountain, burns the calf, grinds it to powder, strews it upon the water and makes the children of Israel drink it. All of that is his brother's doing, not Aaron's; Aaron's part ended at the altar. Then Moses turns on him and asks what the people did to him that he brought so great a sin upon them, and Aaron answers with the crowd, the earrings, and the fire. Three thousand fall by the swords of the Levites, and a plague follows after.
stops.quote: Let not the anger of my lord wax hot: thou knowest the people, that they are set on mischief. For they said unto me, Make us gods, which shall go before us: for as for this Moses, the man that brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we wot not what is become of him. And I said unto them, Whosoever hath any gold, let them break it off. So they gave it me: then I cast it into the fire, and there came out this calf.
suggested_refs: Deuteronomy 9:20, where Moses says the Lord was angry enough with Aaron to destroy him

stops.name: The door of the tent, seven days of ordination
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed. Exodus 40:17 dates the raising of the tabernacle to the first day of the first month of the second year; the seven days of Leviticus 8 therefore precede it, and standard rabbinic chronology runs them from 23 to 29 Adar, with the eighth day of Leviticus 9 falling on 1 Nisan.
stops.campa: For seven days Moses does to Aaron what the Lord commanded him. He washes him with water at the door of the tent, puts on him the coat and the robe and the ephod and the breastplate, sets the mitre on his head and the holy crown upon the mitre, and pours the anointing oil on his head. The ram of consecration is killed and its blood put upon the tip of Aaron's right ear, upon the thumb of his right hand, upon the great toe of his right foot, and upon his sons after him. Seven days they do not go out of the door.
suggested_refs: Leviticus 8, the ordination rite, and Exodus 29 where it is commanded in advance

stops.name: The tabernacle, the eighth day and the strange fire
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed as 1 Nisan of the second year, following Rashi on Leviticus 9:1 and Seder Olam; Leviticus itself says only the eighth day.
stops.campa: On the eighth day Aaron lifts up his hand toward the people and blesses them, and fire comes out from before the Lord and consumes the burnt offering upon the altar, and all the people shout and fall on their faces. Then Nadab and Abihu take their censers and offer strange fire before the Lord, which he commanded them not, and fire goes out from the same place and devours them. Their bodies are carried out of the camp in their coats, and Moses tells his brother what the Lord meant by it.
suggested_refs: Leviticus 10:1-7, the death of Nadab and Abihu

stops.name: The tabernacle, no wine before the Lord
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the same day or the day after the deaths, by narrative sequence in Leviticus 10.
stops.campa: The Lord speaks to Aaron directly, one of the very few times in the book that he is addressed alone and not through his brother: do not drink wine nor strong drink, thou nor thy sons with thee, when ye go into the tabernacle of the congregation, lest ye die. He is to put difference between holy and unholy, between clean and unclean, and to teach the children of Israel the statutes. The same day Moses finds the goat of the sin offering burnt instead of eaten, and is angry with the two sons who are left.
stops.quote: Behold, this day have they offered their sin offering and their burnt offering before the Lord; and such things have befallen me: and if I had eaten the sin offering to day, should it have been accepted in the sight of the Lord?
suggested_refs: Leviticus 10:8-20, the priestly sobriety law and the dispute over the sin offering

stops.name: The wilderness of Sinai, the Levites given to Aaron
stops.date_confidence: attested as an internal biblical date (first day of the second month of the second year, Numbers 1:1); the absolute year is traditional.
stops.campa: The tribe of Levi is numbered apart from the rest of Israel and given to Aaron and to his sons, to keep the charge of the tabernacle and to do the service of it, and the stranger that cometh nigh is to be put to death. The Kohathites carry the ark and the vessels, the Gershonites the curtains, the Merarites the boards and the sockets and the pins. The priesthood itself is two men and their father. Eleazar and Ithamar hold it, and there are no other sons left to hold it with them.
suggested_refs: Numbers 3 and 4, the registration of the Levites under Aaron and his sons

stops.name: Hazeroth, the word spoken against Moses
stops.date_confidence: traditional; after the departure from Sinai on the twentieth day of the second month, Numbers 10:11. The identification of Hazeroth with Ain Khadra is traditional and uncertain.
stops.campa: At Hazeroth Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman he has married, and they say, hath the Lord indeed spoken only by Moses, hath he not spoken also by us. The Lord hears it and calls the three of them out to the door of the tabernacle, and when the cloud departs Miriam is leprous, white as snow. Aaron is untouched. He turns to the brother he has just been challenging, calls him my lord, and asks that the sin not be laid upon them, and she is shut out of the camp seven days.
stops.quote: Alas, my lord, I beseech thee, lay not the sin upon us, wherein we have done foolishly, and wherein we have sinned.
suggested_refs: Ain Khadra in eastern Sinai, traditional site of Hazeroth

stops.name: Kadesh-barnea, the spies and the faces to the ground
stops.date_confidence: traditional; forty days after the spies go up, Numbers 13:25. Kadesh-barnea is identified with Ein el-Qudeirat by leading archaeological opinion; Numbers 13:26 places Kadesh in the wilderness of Paran and Numbers 20:1 in the wilderness of Zin, a tension medieval commentators resolved by positing two Kadeshes.
stops.campa: The spies come back from the land after forty days with grapes carried on a staff between two men, and a report that the people there are giants and the cities walled up to heaven. The congregation weeps all night, talks of choosing a captain to take them back into Egypt, and talks of stoning the brothers. Moses and Aaron fall on their faces before the whole assembly of the congregation of the children of Israel. The sentence comes down that day: a year of wandering for each day the spies were out.
suggested_refs: Ein el-Qudeirat, the spring identified with Kadesh-barnea

stops.name: Kadesh, the earth opens under Korah
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Numbers gives no date for the rebellion, and its position in the wilderness years is inferred from the surrounding narrative.
stops.campa: Korah of the sons of Kohath, with Dathan and Abiram and two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly, rises up and says, ye take too much upon you, seeing all the congregation are holy, every one of them. The test is set for the morning: every man with his censer and his incense, and the Lord will show whose priesthood this is. The ground cleaves asunder under Dathan and Abiram and swallows them and their households, and fire consumes the two hundred and fifty. The sons of Korah, Numbers notes later, did not die.
suggested_refs: Sandro Botticelli, The Punishment of Korah, Sistine Chapel
Numbers 26:11 and the Korahite psalm superscriptions

stops.name: Kadesh, standing between the dead and the living
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the day after the rebellion in narrative sequence, undated in the text.
stops.campa: On the morrow the whole congregation murmurs against Moses and against Aaron, saying, ye have killed the people of the Lord, and the plague begins among them. Moses tells his brother to take a censer, put fire in it from off the altar, put on incense, and go quickly into the congregation. Aaron runs. He stands between the dead and the living with the incense burning in his hands, and the plague is stayed. Fourteen thousand and seven hundred are already dead, beside them that died about the matter of Korah.
suggested_refs: Numbers 16:41-50, the censer that halts the plague

stops.name: The tent of the testimony, the rod with ripe almonds
stops.date_confidence: traditional; undated in Numbers. The episode follows Korah, and is pinned here at the Kadesh encampment rather than at Sinai, since Israel left Sinai in Numbers 10.
stops.campa: Twelve rods are written with twelve names, one for each house of the fathers, and Aaron's name upon the rod of Levi, and they are laid up before the testimony in the tabernacle overnight. In the morning Moses brings them out to all the princes and every man takes his own. Aaron's rod alone has budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds, three seasons at once upon one piece of cut wood. It is put back before the testimony and kept there, for a token against the rebels.
suggested_refs: Numbers 17, the budding rod kept before the ark

stops.name: The wilderness, a covenant of salt and no ground at all
stops.date_confidence: traditional; undated in Numbers, placed after the vindication of the rod by narrative sequence.
stops.campa: The Lord speaks to Aaron: thou shalt have no inheritance in their land, neither shalt thou have any part among them. Every other tribe will be measured a territory with boundaries and towns. In place of ground he is given the heave offerings, the first fruits of the oil and the wine and the wheat, everything devoted in Israel, the firstborn of the clean beasts and the redemption price of the firstborn of men. It is a statute for ever, and the Lord calls it a covenant of salt.
suggested_refs: Numbers 18:8-20, the priestly portions and the covenant of salt

stops.name: Kadesh, the grave of Miriam
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed. Numbers 20:1 says only in the first month and gives no year; the fortieth year is inferred from the Numbers 33 itinerary and from Seder Olam Rabbah 9.
stops.campa: In the first month the children of Israel come again into the wilderness of Zin and abide in Kadesh, and Miriam dies there and is buried there. She is the sister who stood at a distance by the river to see what would be done to the youngest of the three, and who sang with the timbrel on the far shore of the sea. Aaron is a hundred and twenty-two years old and has buried two of his four sons already. Of the house of Amram, Moses and Aaron are left.
suggested_refs: Numbers 20:1, the death of Miriam at Kadesh

stops.name: Meribah, the rock struck twice
stops.date_confidence: traditional; undated in Numbers, placed immediately after Miriam's death by narrative sequence.
stops.campa: There is no water for the congregation at Kadesh and the people gather themselves together against Moses and against Aaron. The Lord says, take the rod, and speak ye unto the rock before their eyes, and it shall give forth his water. Moses says, hear now, ye rebels, must we fetch you water out of this rock, and smites the rock twice with the rod. The water comes out abundantly and the congregation drinks, and their beasts. The sentence that follows falls on Aaron as well as on Moses.
stops.quote: Because you did not trust in me, to show my holiness before the eyes of the Israelites, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them.
suggested_refs: The waters of Meribah at Kadesh, Numbers 20:2-13

stops.name: The border of Edom, passage refused
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the text gives no date and no waypoint between Kadesh and Mount Hor, so these coordinates are an approximate placement on the route.
stops.campa: Messengers go from Kadesh to the king of Edom, reminding him of all the travail that has befallen his brother Israel and asking leave to pass along the king's highway. They promise to turn neither to the right hand nor to the left, to keep out of the fields and the vineyards, and to pay for any water they or their cattle drink. Edom is the house of Esau, kin to Jacob, and the refusal is a family matter. He comes out against them with much people and with a strong hand. Israel turns away from him and goes the long way round, east and south.
suggested_refs: Numbers 20:14-21, the embassy to Edom and its refusal

stops.name: Mount Hor, the garments taken off
stops.date_confidence: attested as an internal biblical date (first day of the fifth month of the fortieth year, Numbers 33:38), which Jewish tradition keeps as the first of Av; the absolute year is traditional, and the identification of Mount Hor with Jabal Harun near Petra is post-biblical.
stops.campa: At the edge of the land of Edom the Lord tells Moses to take Aaron and Eleazar his son up into the mountain, in the sight of all the congregation. The three of them go up. On the top Moses strips his brother of the garments he first put on him at the door of the tent, the coat, the robe, the ephod, the breastplate with the twelve stones, and puts them upon Eleazar. Aaron dies there on the top of the mount, a hundred and twenty-three years old, and Moses and Eleazar come down.
stops.quote: And strip Aaron of his garments, and put them upon Eleazar his son: and Aaron shall be gathered unto his people, and shall die there.
suggested_refs: Jabal Harun above Petra, traditional Mount Hor

stops.name: Moserah, the other grave
stops.date_confidence: contradictory. Deuteronomy 10:6 places the death and burial at Moserah, while Numbers 33:30-31 lists Moseroth as a separate station reached long before Mount Hor; the site is unidentified and these coordinates are a rough placement in the Kadesh-to-Hor corridor.
stops.campa: Deuteronomy, telling the forty years over again, puts the death somewhere else: the children of Israel journeyed from Beeroth of the children of Jaakan to Mosera, there Aaron died, and there he was buried, and Eleazar his son ministered in the priest's office in his stead. The itinerary in Numbers lists Moseroth as a camp reached many stations earlier. The Torah sets the two accounts down side by side and harmonizes neither. Which of the two places holds the grave is a question the text does not take up.
suggested_refs: Deuteronomy 10:6 against Numbers 20:22-29 and 33:38-39, an unresolved contradiction in the Torah

stops.name: The camp below the mountain, thirty days of mourning
stops.date_confidence: traditional; thirty days from the death of Numbers 33:38.
stops.campa: When all the congregation sees that Aaron is dead, they mourn for him thirty days, all the house of Israel, the men and the women both. The mourning for Moses at the end of the same year will also be thirty days, but the rabbis mark the difference in the wording and hold that the whole people wept for Aaron because he was the one who went between quarreling men, and between husbands and wives, and made them friends again. The clouds of glory, they say, lift from the camp on the day he dies.
suggested_refs: b. Taanit 9a on the clouds of glory and the merit of Aaron

stops.name: The Temple Mount, the priesthood comes indoors
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the dedication of Solomon's temple as dated elsewhere in the corpus.
stops.campa: Four centuries on, the priesthood of Aaron's house moves indoors. Solomon finishes the temple at Jerusalem and the sons of Aaron carry into it the offices worked out at a tent in the wilderness: the ephod, the breastplate of judgment, the incense, the daily fire. The legend of the stone-cutting worm that builds the house without iron circles back to the same vestment, since it was with that worm, the tale says, that the stones of the ephod were graven. The rod and the pot of manna lie in the ark in the oracle.
suggested_refs: Hebrews 9:4, which places the budding rod inside the ark alongside the manna and the tables

stops.name: Jerusalem, the disciples of Aaron
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Hillel's floruit in the late first century BC, the saying itself preserved in a Mishnah redacted about 200 CE.
stops.campa: More than a thousand years after the mountain, in a Jerusalem with a second temple and a priesthood that traces its charter to him, Hillel hands his students a saying that will fix Aaron for the whole of Jewish memory afterward. It says nothing about the ephod, the incense, the rod, or the plagues. The man who cast the calf, and who ran into a plague with a censer in his hands, is handed down as the peacemaker, and the later legends fill in whole marriages and quarrels he is supposed to have mended.
stops.quote: Be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace, loving your fellow creatures and bringing them near to the Torah.
suggested_refs: Avot de-Rabbi Natan, which expands the peacemaking legends of Aaron at length

stops.name: Rome, Josephus climbs the mountain again
stops.date_confidence: attested to within a year or two; the Jewish Antiquities are conventionally dated to 93 or 94 CE.
stops.campa: In Rome, writing the whole history of his nation for Greek readers who have just finished destroying it, Josephus climbs Mount Hor again. He has Moses lead his brother up in the sight of the multitude, strip him of the high priest's robes, and put them on Eleazar, and Aaron die apart on the height while the army waits below. Numbers names no neighbouring city and no range. Josephus names the mountain as the one that encloses Petra, and the pilgrim roads to the grave all start from that sentence.
suggested_refs: Flavius Josephus, Jewish Antiquities IV.4.7, the earliest text tying Aaron's tomb to the Petra region
sources: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews IV.4.7

stops.name: Jabal Harun, the house of the Saint High-Priest Aaron
stops.date_confidence: attested for the document of 573 CE; the memorial church is dated by excavation to the fifth century, and the monastic complex sits on the saddle west of the summit rather than on the peak itself.
stops.campa: On the saddle west of the peak the Christians build: a basilica, a chapel, a hostel for pilgrims, cisterns cut into a mountain that has no water of its own. A document of 573 in the carbonized church archive at Petra calls the place the House of our Lord the Saint High-Priest Aaron. The Finnish excavators date the memorial church to the fifth century. Pottery and coin from the terrace run from the Byzantine centuries into the early Islamic ones without a break.
suggested_refs: The Petra Papyri, carbonized sixth-century archive of the Petra church
The Finnish Jabal Harun Project excavation reports
sources: Z. T. Fiema and J. Frosen, Petra: The Mountain of Aaron (Finnish Jabal Harun Project)

stops.name: Troyes, the commentator at the verse
stops.date_confidence: attested; Rashi died at Troyes in 1105, and the Torah commentary was written there over the preceding decades.
stops.campa: In a vineyard town in Champagne with a small Jewish community and a school in it, Solomon ben Isaac writes a running commentary on the whole Torah, and it is through Rashi's voice that most later readers will meet Aaron at all. He is the one who explains why the elder brother rejoiced instead of resenting, how the calf came out of the fire, why the seven days of ordination fall in Adar. Every difficulty in the text gets a few words of answer. The commentary is printed beside the text in every rabbinic Bible from 1475 onward.
suggested_refs: Rashi's commentary on Exodus and Leviticus, printed alongside the text in every rabbinic Bible since 1475
sources: Rashi, commentary on Exodus and Leviticus

stops.name: Jabal Harun, the white dome on the summit
stops.date_confidence: uncertain within the Mamluk period. A construction date of 1458 or 1459 circulates with an attribution to the sultan Qaitbay, which is impossible since he reigned only from 1468; the reigning sultan in 1459 was al-Ashraf Inal, and no patron is securely attested.
stops.campa: A small white domed building goes up on the summit in the Mamluk centuries, over whatever stood there before it, and the mountain is called Jabal Harun, Aaron's mountain, by everyone who lives in sight of it. Jews, Christians and Muslims all keep the tradition of the grave. The Quran names Harun a prophet given to his brother out of mercy, and Bedouin families climb up to slaughter and to make vows at the shrine. Whose hand raised the dome, and in which sultan's reign, is not securely known.
suggested_refs: The Maqam Nabi Harun on the summit of Jabal Harun, a shared shrine of three religions

stops.name: Jabal Harun, the traveller who came to sacrifice a goat
stops.date_confidence: attested; Burckhardt reached the Petra valley on 22 August 1812, and his account was published posthumously in 1822.
stops.campa: A Swiss traveller in Arab dress, calling himself Sheikh Ibrahim, tells his guides that he has vowed to sacrifice a goat at the tomb of Harun, and on that pretext is taken up a gorge past the carved facades of a city no European has reported in centuries. Petra enters European scholarship on this walk, and he dares not stop to examine any of it closely. He sees the shrine on the summit from below, is hurried along by men who suspect him of hunting treasure, and kills the goat short of the top. He never reaches the tomb.
suggested_refs: Johann Ludwig Burckhardt, Travels in Syria and the Holy Land (1822)
sources: Burckhardt, Travels in Syria and the Holy Land (1822)
